sources.title: U7-U11 source discovery and question seeds
sources.sectionOrPage: Source receipts; Conflicts and holds for the catalog compiler
sources.supports: Records the previously inspected Hockey Canada and USA Hockey youth sources and their bounded use for U7-U11 topic placement, scanning, retrieval and movement recognition.
sources.doesNotSupport: Does not approve any authored answer, infer a digital scoring rule, or certify skating/scanning/live transfer from a static scene.
sources.ageJurisdiction: U7-U11; Hockey Canada program context plus USA Hockey age-context evidence; not a universal Canadian rules crosswalk.
sources.conflicts: The note records a Hockey Canada U9 full-ice transition-date conflict between FAQ and rules pages; this pilot contains no date-dependent rule item.

sources.title: U13-U18 source discovery
sources.supports: Provides local provenance and limits for age-context skating, support, transition and retrieval themes; explicitly separates topic fit from invented-scene answer logic.
sources.doesNotSupport: Does not provide a validated U13 pace-change answer, speed threshold, route outcome, or technique assessment.
sources.ageJurisdiction: U13-U18 proposed adaptation bands; Hockey Canada and USA Hockey sources with jurisdiction/context boundaries.
sources.conflicts: The document distinguishes directly opened sources from USA Hockey indexed text and warns that public previews of Jack Han material are inspiration only.

sources.title: Skating Skill Development | The Skating Pathway
sources.sectionOrPage: Continue to build the Skating Foundation; Keys to teaching skating; Eight specialized skating skills
sources.supports: Hockey Canada says basic skating is introduced at Timbits U7/U9, developed at U11/U13/U15 and refined at U18+, with age-specific progressive technique and game-like progressions. It lists agility/balance, edge control, turning, transition and quick feet.
sources.doesNotSupport: A still image cannot demonstrate or score speed, acceleration, edge control, stopping, turning, pivot execution, or a successful evasion. The page's instruction to use repetitions and progressions is practice guidance, not static-scene evidence.
sources.ageJurisdiction: Hockey Canada player-development pathway; age labels are Canadian program context.
sources.conflicts: No material conflict for this pilot; the page's broad age progression does not establish a single correct movement choice in an authored scene.

sources.title: 7 Principles for Coaches: Vision & Scanning
sources.sectionOrPage: Key Information to Identify; Incorporating Vision Into Training; Reading Pressure / Corner Situations
sources.supports: Hockey Canada identifies teammate locations and the source of opposition pressure as the two key information sources. It says scanning is taught at all ages and gives corner progressions including shoulder-check turn pressure and absorb-and-spin from pressure.
sources.doesNotSupport: The page does not establish a mandatory scan interval, prove that a player actually scanned, or make a particular outlet/escape successful from a freeze. Its drills are training progressions, not answer keys.
sources.ageJurisdiction: Hockey Canada coaching guidance presented for all ages; apply one visible cue and age-appropriate complexity for U11.
sources.conflicts: No direct conflict; the article says processing speed matters more as game speed increases, which qualifies but does not measure the pilot's U11 scene.

sources.title: FUNdamentals Stage — ADM
sources.sectionOrPage: pp.1-3: objective, key focus, progression, small-area games and U8 environment
sources.supports: USA Hockey places ages 6-8 female/6-9 male in a fundamentals stage: refine fundamental movement skills, introduce basic puck control, use proper progression, and use cross-ice/half-ice games focused on skill development rather than outcomes.
sources.doesNotSupport: It cannot validate a particular turn/space answer, prove a child has speed or balance from a picture, or transfer a US age-stage statement into a Canadian program rule.
sources.ageJurisdiction: USA Hockey ADM; ages 6-8 female and 6-9 male, used here as age-context corroboration for U7/U9 concepts.
sources.conflicts: Age bands and program formats differ from Hockey Canada; retain the pilot's declared age labels and do not infer Canadian rules.

sources.title: Learn to Train Stage — ADM
sources.sectionOrPage: pp.1-5: skill acquisition, small-area decision making, deception and tactical roles
sources.supports: USA Hockey places ages 8-11 female/9-12 male in Learn to Train, emphasizing solid skating/puck-control skills, short agility/change-of-direction work, small-area games for decision making, and later-stage deception including change of pace/direction.
sources.doesNotSupport: The document does not prove that a static U11/U13 freeze contains enough motion to assess pace change, acceleration, pivot or edge technique, nor that one route is universally correct.
sources.ageJurisdiction: USA Hockey ADM; U11/U13 use requires adaptation across US age bands and Canadian labels.
sources.conflicts: Its US competition formats and age bands are not Canadian policy; only development themes are transferred.

findings.claim: The U7/U9 skating scenes are age-topic appropriate as recognition/discussion prompts.
findings.evidence: Hockey Canada introduces basic skating at U7/U9 and lists turning/transition; USA Hockey 8U emphasizes fundamentals, progression and skill-focused small-area play.
findings.implication: Keep questions about visible relationships, declared movement ideas or discussion routines. Do not score technique from the freeze.

findings.claim: U11/U13 pivot and pace-change themes are developmentally plausible, but the static authored scenes only support movement-decision discussion.
findings.evidence: Hockey Canada progresses skating development through U11/U13 and USA Hockey 12U includes agility/change of direction, decision making and deception/change of pace.
findings.implication: Repair any wording that implies measured speed, acceleration, successful evasion, or demonstrated pivot mechanics. Accept grounded comparisons of pressure, support and open space, with more than one reasonable discussion choice where geometry permits.

findings.claim: The U11 retrieval-scan scenario has direct source support for identifying teammate availability and pressure source.
findings.evidence: Hockey Canada's 2024 article names teammate location and opposition pressure as the two key scanning inputs and describes corner pressure progressions.
findings.implication: Retain cue-identification, changed-cue and explain-reasoning prompts. Label them as observation/discussion; a freeze cannot prove the player scanned or that a pass/pickup succeeds.

findings.claim: No reviewed source supports admitting a static 3D scene as a skating-technique or live-performance assessment.
findings.evidence: The local discovery notes explicitly separate topic evidence from answer logic; the public Hockey Canada and USA Hockey documents describe progressive training and drills, not screenshot certification.
findings.implication: Keep the existing admission limits and coach-calibration status. Exact repairs should target wording and answer multiplicity, not silently upgrade source support.
